**Observation Log:**

- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/24 (Wed) 12:24
- [USER] The user discussed the historical problem of the quadrature of the circle.
- [USER] The user mentioned that the problem involves constructing a square with the same area as a given circle.
- [USER] The user noted the divine nature of the circle and orb, and the construction of a cube similar in content to a given orb.
- [USER] The user stated that the difficulty of the problem added to the mysterious nature of the circle and encouraged mysticism.
- [USER] The user referenced Hippocrates of Chios (470 - 410) as one of the oldest known philosophers who attempted to solve the quadrature of the circle.
- [USER] The user described Hippocrates as a wealthy merchant with an appetite for geometria.
- [USER] The user claimed that Hippocrates was allegedly the first to determine the height of the Egyptian pyramids by measuring their shadows and using similarity.
- [USER] The user mentioned that most knowledge about Hippocrates comes from writings of people decades after his death.
- [USER] The user referred to the "moons of Hippocrates" as a known attempt to solve the quadrature of the circle.
- [USER] The user explained that Hippocrates showed that moon-shaped figures bounded by different circle segments could be quadrated easily.
- [USER] The user concluded that Hippocrates' approach turned out to be a dead end.
- [USER] The user introduced Euclid's "The Elements" as a significant work related to the quadrature of the circle.
- [USER] The user noted that Euclid was active around 300 BC in Alexandria, Egypt.
- [USER] The user stated that "The Elements" has influenced the history of Western culture and is one of the most well-known texts from antiquity.
- [USER] The user emphasized that "The Elements" was not a textbook as we know it today, but was written and copied, never printed.
- [USER] The user explained that pre-printing press culture did not allow for exact copies and that surviving copies show many similarities but are not the same.
- [USER] The user mentioned that commentaries written in the margins by philosophers or pupils studying the text sometimes became part of the text itself.
- [USER] The user highlighted that we do not know what the original text by Euclid looked like, with closest examples being Arabian sources produced centuries later.
- [USER] The user pointed out that the modern understanding of "geometria" differs from ancient ideas.
- [USER] The user noted that "The Elements" introduces the elementary parts of geometria, starting with definitions and axioms.
- [USER] The user described Euclid's axioms as reflecting the necessities and possibilities of constructing objects in an ideal world.
